title: Multiprotocol Label Switching Architecture
summary: Describes the architecture of Multiprotocol Label Switching, where routers forward packets using short labels instead of examining full IP destination addresses at every hop. It explains label switched paths and the roles of routers. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: Instead of reading the full address at every stop, a traveler follows color-coded tags that say which way to go next. This explains how the tag system works.

questions: what is a forwarding equivalence class
what is an mpls label stack
what is a label switched path
subtitle: How routers can forward packets by swapping short labels instead of re-reading IP addresses at every hop.

tldr.problem: In conventional IP forwarding every router analyzes each packet's header and runs a routing algorithm to pick the next hop, even though the header holds far more information than that choice needs.
tldr.mechanism: MPLS assigns a packet to a Forwarding Equivalence Class once, when it enters the network, and encodes that class as a short fixed length label. Later routers use the label as an index into a table that gives the next hop and a new label.
tldr.outcome: This architecture document defines the vocabulary, forwarding tables, label distribution procedures and tunnelling rules for MPLS. It is a Proposed Standard that has since been updated by RFC 6178 and RFC 6790.

today: RFC 3031 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted, but it is updated by RFC 6178 and RFC 6790. The RFC itself leaves multicast use of MPLS for further study.

sections.title: Why Forward by Label
sections.content:
As a packet crosses a network, each router normally analyzes its header and independently chooses a next hop. Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) splits that choice in two: one function sorts all possible packets into Forwarding Equivalence Classes (FECs), and a second maps each FEC to a next hop. Packets in the same FEC are indistinguishable as far as forwarding goes.

In MPLS the assignment to a FEC happens just once, as the packet enters the network. The FEC is encoded as a short fixed length value called a label that travels with the packet. At later hops there is no further analysis of the network layer header. The label is an index into a table that returns the next hop and a new label, the old label is replaced, and the packet moves on. A router that supports MPLS is a Label Switching Router (LSR).

The RFC lists several benefits. Simple switches that can do label lookup but cannot analyze network headers fast enough can still forward. The ingress router may use any information it has, such as the arrival port, to pick the FEC. Increasingly complicated FEC rules do not burden routers that only forward labeled packets. And an explicit route can be represented by a label, so it does not have to be carried in every packet as with source routing.

The word Multiprotocol reflects that the techniques apply to any network layer protocol, although the document focuses on IP. The use of MPLS for multicast is left for further study.
sections.eli5: Normally every post office reads the whole address on your letter. With MPLS the first post office sticks on a small colored sticker, and every office after that just follows the sticker.

sections.title: Labels, Bindings and Label Distribution
sections.content:
A label is a short, fixed length, locally significant identifier for a FEC. Most often a packet's FEC depends on its destination address, but the label is never an encoding of that address. Two LSRs can agree that when upstream LSR Ru sends a packet to downstream LSR Rd, it labels the packet with value L if and only if the packet belongs to FEC F. That agreement is a binding, and L has meaning only between Ru and Rd. Each LSR must be able to interpret its incoming labels uniquely.

Bindings are made by the downstream LSR and passed to the upstream LSR, so labels are downstream-assigned. A set of procedures by which LSRs tell each other their bindings is a label distribution protocol, and LSRs that exchange bindings are label distribution peers. The architecture does not assume a single such protocol: some existing protocols were extended to carry labels, and new ones were defined for the purpose. The acronym LDP is used here only for the protocol defined in RFC 3036.

Distribution can be downstream-on-demand, where an LSR asks its next hop for a binding, or unsolicited downstream, where bindings are sent without being asked. Both can be used in the same network, but the two peers on one adjacency must agree. An LSR that receives a binding from an LSR that is not its next hop can either keep it (Liberal Label Retention, faster adaptation to routing changes) or discard it (Conservative Label Retention, many fewer labels to maintain).

Labels can be unique per interface when the peers are directly connected over point-to-point interfaces and are the only peers given that value. Otherwise the labels must be unique across the whole LSR, a per-platform label space.
sections.eli5: A label is a small tag that only two neighbors understand. The neighbor closer to the destination picks the tag and tells the neighbor behind it what it means.

sections.title: NHLFE, ILM and FTN: The Forwarding Tables
sections.content:
A packet may carry more than one label. The labels form a last-in, first-out label stack, and an unlabeled packet is one whose stack has depth 0. Processing always uses the top label, whatever else is in the stack.

The Next Hop Label Forwarding Entry (NHLFE) is what an LSR consults to forward a labeled packet. It holds the packet's next hop and an operation on the label stack: replace the top label with a new one, pop the stack, or replace the top label and then push one or more new labels. It may also hold the data link encapsulation, the way to encode the stack and other disposal information. If the next hop is the LSR itself, the operation MUST be a pop, and the LSR then forwards the result again, possibly looking at the IP header.

Two maps lead to NHLFEs. The Incoming Label Map (ILM) maps each incoming label to a set of NHLFEs and is used for packets that arrive labeled. The FEC-to-NHLFE map (FTN) maps each FEC to a set of NHLFEs and is used for packets that arrive unlabeled but are to be labeled. When a set has several entries, exactly one is chosen before forwarding, for example to balance load over equal-cost paths; how is outside the document.

Using these tables is called label swapping. The RFC stresses that the next hop is always taken from the NHLFE, which may differ from what plain routing would choose.
sections.eli5: A router keeps a small cheat sheet. Find the tag on the packet, and the sheet says where to send it and what tag to put on next.

sections.title: LSPs, Tunnels and Penultimate Hop Popping
sections.content:
A Label Switched Path (LSP) is the sequence of routers a packet follows while being switched on a label at one level of the stack. It starts at the LSP ingress, which pushes a label, and ends at the LSP egress, where the decision is made on a lower-level label or by ordinary forwarding. LSPs for one FEC from many ingresses that share an egress can be viewed as a multipoint-to-point tree rooted at the egress.

With penultimate hop popping, the next-to-last LSR removes the label, so the egress needs only one lookup instead of two. The penultimate node pops only if the egress requests it or if the next node does not support MPLS. An LSR that is able to pop MUST do so when its downstream peer asks, and an LSR MUST NOT request popping from a peer unless that peer is capable. The special Implicit NULL label is how an egress asks for this.

A tunnel is created when a router makes a packet reach a router that is not the next hop on its normal path. An LSP can serve as the tunnel, and tunnels nest to any depth because of the label stack. In the RFC's example a packet crosses the tunnel between R2 and R3 by having R2 swap the level 1 label and push a level 2 label, with the last tunnel router popping it.

Applications in section 4 build on this. Explicitly routed LSP tunnels support policy routing and traffic engineering. Hop-by-hop routed LSP tunnels between BGP border routers let interior routers carry transit traffic without holding the BGP routes. One label can stand for several address prefixes with the same egress (egress-targeted label assignment) to reduce label counts, and a level 2 label can ride as a Stack Attribute of a level 1 binding.
sections.eli5: Imagine the packet riding a train line. A tunnel is a smaller shuttle line inside the big line, and a second sticker tells the shuttle where to go, then comes off when the shuttle ends.

sections.title: TTL, Loops and Unusable Labels
sections.content:
If an LSR gets a labeled packet whose incoming label has no binding, it is tempting to strip the label and forward the IP packet. The RFC says this can cause a loop, so the packet MUST be discarded unless some other means shows that forwarding it unlabeled is harmless. The same advice applies when the label is valid but the ILM gives no outgoing entry: unless it can be shown to be safe, the only safe procedure is to discard.

IP uses a Time To Live (TTL) value to limit loops and to support things like traceroute. A packet leaving an LSP SHOULD have the TTL it would have had without label switching. If labels live in a shim header, the shim MUST have a TTL field that SHOULD be loaded from the network header, decremented at each LSR hop and copied back at the end of the LSP.

Where labels sit in a link layer header such as ATM, the hardware cannot decrement a TTL. Such a run of LSRs is a non-TTL LSP segment. The packet SHOULD still emerge with a TTL that reflects the hops it took, and if its TTL would expire inside the segment, the ingress LSR must not label switch it. Because loops are then not limited by TTL, all LSRs that attach to non-TTL segments are required to support a common loop detection technique, though using it is optional.
sections.eli5: If a router sees a tag it does not know, it should throw the packet away rather than guess, because guessing might send it in circles.

sections.title: Label Encodings and Merging
sections.content:
The architecture needs a concrete way to carry a label stack and allows several. With MPLS-specific hardware or software the natural choice is a protocol-independent shim between the data link and network layer headers, specified in RFC 3032. Legacy ATM switches can also act as LSRs, since they already swap an incoming VPI/VCI for an outgoing one. The RFC lists three ways to put labels in an ATM cell header: SVC encoding, SVP encoding and SVP multipoint encoding. If there are more labels than the ATM header can hold, the ATM encoding must be combined with the generic encapsulation. Different hops of one LSP may use different encodings, but two ATM switches that can be successive LSRs must use the same one.

Label merging means sending packets of one FEC that arrived with different labels or on different interfaces out with a single label. With merging, an LSR needs only one outgoing label per FEC. Without it, the count could grow as large as the number of nodes in the network. ATM switches using SVC or SVP encoding cannot merge, because interleaved cells from different packets could not be reassembled.

MPLS therefore supports both merging and non-merging LSRs. A non-merging upstream neighbor is given a label only when it explicitly asks, and may ask repeatedly for new ones. Over ATM, merging can use VP merge, where packets from different sources are told apart by VCI, or VC merge, where a switch buffers cells until the whole packet has arrived.
sections.eli5: There is more than one way to stick the tag on a packet. Merging is like several small streams flowing into one river that carries a single tag.

sections.title: Label Distribution Procedures
sections.content:
Two broad choices shape how LSPs are set up. With independent LSP control, each LSR binds a label to a FEC and tells its peers on its own, like conventional IP routing. With ordered LSP control, an LSR binds only if it is the egress or has already received a binding from its next hop. Ordered control must be used when traffic has to follow a path with specified properties, and the two modes interoperate.

Section 5 splits label distribution into procedures. The downstream LSR runs the Distribution procedure (four variants) and the Withdraw procedure (one). The upstream LSR runs the Request procedure (RequestNever, RequestWhenNeeded, RequestOnRequest), the NotAvailable procedure (RequestRetry, RequestNoRetry), the Release procedure (ReleaseOnChange, NoReleaseOnChange) and the labelUse procedure (UseImmediate, UseIfLoopNotDetected). Withdrawn bindings must always be withdrawn explicitly, and an unbinding of L from X must reach the peer before L is bound to any other prefix.

A choice of one variant per procedure is a quintuple called an MPLS scheme. Only listed combinations are supported: seven for LSRs that support merging and three for those that do not. Some quintuples cannot work, for example any scheme where the downstream LSR sends labels only on request but the upstream LSR never requests. Peers state at initialization whether they support merging, and a non-merging peer's preferences take priority. If both merge, the upstream LSR chooses liberal or conservative retention, and the downstream LSR chooses push or pull and conditional or unconditional.

The route for a FEC may be chosen hop by hop or explicitly, either strictly or loosely, by a single LSR such as the ingress or egress. Explicit routing needs the route given only when labels are assigned, not in every packet, which the RFC says makes it more efficient than IP source routing. Aggregation, binding one label to a union of FECs, reduces the number of labels and the amount of control traffic.
sections.eli5: Neighbors have rules for who offers tags, who asks, and when to forget old ones. This part lists the rule sets that are allowed to work together.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security section is short and raises two points. First, some routers rely on the network layer header being at a fixed place after the data link header for security procedures. The generic MPLS encapsulation inserts a shim between the two, which may make such procedures fail.

Second, a label has meaning only because of an agreement between the LSR that writes it and the LSR that reads it. If labeled packets are accepted from untrusted sources, or if an incoming label is accepted from an LSR to which that label was not distributed, packets may be routed in an illegitimate manner.
sections.eli5: A tag only works if both neighbors agreed on what it means. If a stranger can stick tags on packets, they could send them to the wrong place.

viz.caption: TWO WAYS TO PICK A NEXT HOP

left.title: Conventional IP forwarding
left.desc: Each router analyzes the packet header, runs a routing algorithm and independently chooses a next hop.

right.title: MPLS forwarding
right.desc: The packet gets a label once at entry. Later routers look the label up, swap it for a new one and forward.

items.title: NHLFE
items.text: The next hop plus an operation on the label stack: replace the top label, pop, or replace and push.

items.title: ILM
items.text: Maps an incoming label to a set of NHLFEs. Used for packets that arrive labeled.

items.title: FTN
items.text: Maps a FEC to a set of NHLFEs. Used for packets that arrive unlabeled but must be labeled.

items.title: Shim header
items.text: A protocol-independent shim between the data link and network layer headers (RFC 3032).

items.title: ATM SVC encoding
items.text: Top label in the VPI/VCI field. ATM-LSRs cannot push or pop and cannot merge.

items.title: ATM SVP encoding
items.text: Top label in the VPI field and second label in the VCI field. Not usable across a non-MPLS ATM virtual path.

items.title: ATM SVP multipoint
items.text: Top label in VPI, second label in part of the VCI, and the rest of the VCI identifies the LSP ingress. Allows merging without cell interleave.
